opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. What excites me most is that smell is the one major sense we've never really digitized. We figured out how to capture, store, and reproduce sight and sound over a century ago: cameras, microphones, screens, speakers. Those technologies changed how we live and communicate. But smell has stayed analog. It's locked in the physical world, and for most people it's something you can't measure, can't record, and can't share.

That's a strange gap when you consider how much smell matters. It's tied to memory and emotion more directly than almost any other sense. It shapes what we eat and whom we're drawn to, and it warns us about danger like smoke, spoiled food, or a gas leak. It can even carry signals about health. Doctors have long noticed that certain diseases have characteristic odors, and there are anecdotes of people who can smell conditions like Parkinson's. That suggests there's a huge amount of information in the air around us that we're mostly ignoring.

So the idea of making olfaction available to everyone is really about giving computers a nose. If you can build models that look at a molecule's structure and predict what it smells like, and then pair that with sensors that can detect those molecules, you open up a whole range of possibilities. You could have better tools for food safety and quality, more sustainable ways to discover fragrance ingredients without relying on scarce natural resources, and safer and more effective insect repellents. Further out, you might get early, non-invasive health screening.

And the "everyone" part matters to me. Right now, expertise in smell is concentrated in a small number of highly trained people, like perfumers, flavorists, and sommeliers, who spend years developing that skill. It's beautiful expertise, but it doesn't scale. If machine learning can help encode some of that knowledge, it doesn't replace those people. It lets their insight reach far more places and problems.

For me, it's one of those rare areas where the science is still wide open, the potential impact is enormous, and the tools from AI have finally gotten good enough to make real progress. That combination is pretty thrilling.

r001.rationale: The response describes several potential applications and says the science is wide open, but it does not say that people would invent uses that cannot be anticipated in advance.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me, Sam. What excites me most is that smell is the last of our major senses that computers simply can't deal with. We digitized sight and sound decades ago, and that unlocked cameras in every pocket, voice assistants, entire industries. Smell has been left behind, and yet it's arguably the sense most tied to the chemistry of the world around us, to memory, to emotion, to health.

So when I think about making olfactory technology available to everyone, I think about a few things. One is that every breath you take carries information. Your breath, your skin, the air in your home all contain molecules that tell a story about what's happening, whether that's disease, spoilage, environmental hazards, or just what's for dinner. Right now almost all of that information is thrown away. If we can build sensors and models that read it, we get a whole new channel of data about the physical world that's cheap, continuous, and noninvasive.

The second thing is that this has historically been a really closed, artisanal field. The fragrance and flavor industry has deep expertise, but it's expensive, trained over decades, and not accessible. Giving everyone a map of odor space, a way to predict what a molecule smells like before you make it, lowers the barrier enormously. That's democratizing in the same way that open image models let people who weren't computer vision experts build things.

And honestly, the third is that it's just a fascinating scientific problem. There's no equivalent of RGB for smell. You can't take a scent and decompose it into three primaries. Learning that structure from data, and then seeing it line up with how humans and animals actually perceive odors, has been one of the most rewarding things I've worked on. The idea that we might finally put that in people's hands is what gets me up in the morning.

r001.rationale: The response names possible uses such as detecting disease, spoilage, and hazards, but does not say that people will invent uses that cannot be anticipated in advance.

astra-6.text:
What excites me is that smell is this incredibly rich part of our experience, but we don’t have the tools to work with it the way we do with images or sound. You can take a picture and send it to someone across the world. You can record a song. We don’t have that same ability with smell.

And I’d love to see what happens when more people can build with it. What would an artist do? What would a doctor do? What would someone who’s lost their sense of smell want to create? You can imagine applications in health, food, and everyday enjoyment, but I suspect some of the most interesting ideas will come from people who aren’t working on olfaction today. Giving those people a way to experiment—that’s what’s exciting to me.

r001.rationale: The response invites open-ended ideas and predicts contributions from people outside olfaction, but it does not clearly say that the uses they would invent cannot be fully anticipated in advance.

sol-6.1.text:
What excites me is giving people access to a part of the world that’s incredibly rich, but that we don’t really have tools to understand or share. We can capture an image, record a sound, and send either one across the planet. We can’t do that with smell yet.

And smell matters. It’s connected to food, to memory, to how we experience the people and places around us. If we can make it something that computers can work with, we can give people new ways to create, communicate, and solve problems. I’m especially excited about what people will come up with that we haven’t anticipated. You put a new tool in people’s hands, and they find uses for it that its inventors never imagined.

r001.rationale: The candidate says people will find uses for the tool that its inventors never imagined, clearly conveying that those uses cannot be fully anticipated.
